meta.title: Who really said "Walk far enough and you will meet yourself, coming the other way"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Verified: the line is in The Discworld Companion (1994) by Terry Pratchett and Stephen Briggs. The older saying behind it was in print by 1895.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Walk far enough and you will meet yourself, coming the other way'?
meta.ogDescription: It's genuinely in Pratchett & Briggs's Discworld Companion (1994), describing Lancre's magical caves. But the saying itself is anonymous and was in print by 1895.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1948–2015 · English author of the Discworld novels
answer.sourceLine: The exact wording appears in The Discworld Companion (Gollancz, 1994), which Pratchett co-wrote with Stephen Briggs, in the entry on the caves of Lancre. Pratchett did not invent the idea: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the saying “If you walk far enough you’ll meet yourself” already in circulation by 1895, and nobody knows who first said it.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: The caves are rumoured to run everywhere in the kingdom; it is widely believed that there is a secret entrance in the castle. But they are also one of those features that are not bound by the laws of time and space. Travel far enough in the caves and you will find mythical kings, asleep with their warriors; you will hear the roar of the Minotaur and the sheep of the Cyclops. Walk far enough and you will meet yourself, coming the other way …
trail: Quote Investigator (2022) ↗ traces the whole family of “meet yourself” sayings. It quotes this exact sentence from The Discworld Companion (1994), “Topic: Lancre, Quote Page 138,” and marks it verified with scans.

The Internet Archive’s scan of the 1994 Gollancz edition ↗ is catalogued under Terry Pratchett, with Stephen Briggs as an associated name. A full-text search of the scan returns the sentence word for word, right after the Minotaur and Cyclops lines.
Wikipedia ↗ describes the Companion as an encyclopedia of the Discworld created by Pratchett and Briggs, first published by Gollancz in 1994 and reissued in later editions.
The same sentence carries on into later editions, including the Internet Archive’s scan of Turtle Recall: The Discworld Companion … So Far (William Morrow, 2014) ↗.
source.excerptNote: Text as transcribed by Quote Investigator from scans of the 1994 Gollancz edition. The popular quote leaves off the closing ellipsis and everything about the caves, which is why it now reads as a travel or self-discovery saying instead of a joke about magic.

source.rightsNote: This wording comes from The Discworld Companion, first published in 1994. That is well after 1931, so the book is still in copyright in the United States. The short anonymous saying it builds on (“If you walk far enough you’ll meet yourself”) is common phrasing from at least the 1890s and belongs to no one.

author.name: Terry Pratchett
author.heading: About Terry Pratchett
author.bio: Sir Terry Pratchett was an English author, humorist and satirist. He is best known for the Discworld series of 41 comic fantasy novels, published between 1983 and 2015, and for Good Omens (1990), which he co-wrote with Neil Gaiman. With Stephen Briggs he also compiled The Discworld Companion, an encyclopedia of the Discworld that has been updated through several editions.

misattribution.heading: Who else gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This line really does appear in a Pratchett book. The story around it gets garbled, though. People treat it as an original Pratchett insight, and close variants are pinned on other writers.

items.scope: as the person who came up with the idea
items.why: The popular wording comes from his 1994 Companion, co-written with Stephen Briggs. But Quote Investigator ↗ found the saying in The Boston Post in 1895, where a speaker called it “the story they tell.” QI concludes that the originator is unknown.

items.scope: “If you travel far enough, you’ll eventually meet yourself”
items.why: Goodreads cites Campbell’s Myths to Live By, but Quote Investigator ↗ searched that book and the quotation is not in it.

items.scope: “…one day you will recognize yourself coming down the road to meet yourself”
items.why: The Jungian analyst wrote a different version in Addiction to Perfection (1982), which Quote Investigator ↗ verified with scans. She wrote it after the saying was already in use, and it is not Pratchett’s sentence.
In Cloud Atlas (2004) the phrase is used as a password, according to Quote Investigator ↗. That is ten years after the Companion and long after the saying first appeared.

misattribution.truthLine: The words “Walk far enough and you will meet yourself, coming the other way” come from The Discworld Companion (1994) by Terry Pratchett and Stephen Briggs. The idea behind them is an anonymous saying that Quote Investigator ↗ finds in circulation by 1895.

context.heading: What it meant on the page
lead: In the Companion the line is not advice about life. It closes a description of the caves under Lancre, the small mountain kingdom where Pratchett’s witches live. The entry says the caves “are not bound by the laws of time and space”: go deep enough and you find sleeping kings, the Minotaur and the sheep of the Cyclops. Meeting yourself is the last and strangest stop on that tour.

Cut loose from that context and stripped of its trailing ellipsis, the sentence now travels as a saying about self-discovery. That is close to how the older anonymous saying was used, which Quote Investigator ↗ finds applied to winding Boston streets, recycled fashions and political circles long before Discworld.
